[[File:BlaineHouse1.JPG|thumb|200px|[[Blaine House]] is the official residence of the governor of Maine. The Executive Mansion was officially declared the residence of the governor in 1919 with the name "The Blaine House". It is located in Augusta, Maine, across the street from the Maine State House.]]
{{History of Maine}}

The [[governor of Maine]] is the [[head of government]] of [[Maine]]. There have been 71 governors since statehood, serving 75 distinct terms. Four governors served multiple non-consecutive terms ([[Edward Kent]], [[John Fairfield]], [[John W. Dana]], and [[Burton M. Cross]]). The longest-serving governor was [[Joseph E. Brennan]], who served two terms from 1979 to 1987. The shortest-serving governors were [[Nathaniel M. Haskell]] and [[Richard H. Vose]], who each served only one day. [[John W. Dana]] also served for one day in 1844, after the incumbent governor resigned, but was later elected to the governorship. The current governor is Democrat [[Janet Mills]], who took office on January 2, 2019.

==Governors==
The [[District of Maine]] of [[Massachusetts]] was [[Admission to the Union|admitted to the Union]] on March 15, 1820, as the State of Maine.<ref>{{usstat|3|544}}</ref>
The [[Constitution of Maine|Maine Constitution]] of 1820 originally established a gubernatorial term of one year,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1656|loc=1820 art. V, pt. 1, § 2}} to begin on the first Wednesday of January; constitutional amendments expanded this to two years in 1879{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1665|loc=1820 art. XXIII}} and to four years in 1957. The 1957 amendment also prohibited governors from succeeding themselves after serving two terms.<ref name="amends">{{cite web |url=https://www.maine.gov/legis/lawlib/lldl/constitutionalamendments/ |title=Maine Constitutional Amendments |access-date=October 28, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260907151615/https://www.maine.gov/legis/lawlib/lldl/constitutionalamendments/ |archive-date=September 7, 2026 |url-status=live |website=[[Maine Legislature]]}}</ref> The constitution does not establish an office of [[lieutenant governor (United States)|lieutenant governor]]; a vacancy in the office of governor is filled by the president of the [[Maine Senate]], who, prior to an amendment in 1964,<ref name="amends" /> only acted as governor.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1657|loc=1820 art. V, pt. 1, § 14}}

|rowspan="2" data-sort-value="742"|January 2, 1839{{sfn|Kallenbach|1977|p=233}}<br/>–<br/>January 12, 1841<br>{{small|(742 days; lost election)}}{{efn|The 1840 election was very close, and the legislature had to decide a winner. Due to the delay, President of the Senate Vose declared himself acting governor on January 12, 1841,<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 14, 1841 |title=Maine Legislature |page=2 |newspaper=[[Bangor Daily News|Bangor Daily Whig and Courier]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/bangor-daily-whig-and-courier-vose-named/120124450/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230927193255/https://www.newspapers.com/article/120124450/vose-named-acting-governor/ |archive-date=September 27, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> under the principle that the office was vacant, so it fell to him.<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 15, 1841 |title=Courtesy vs. the Constitution |page=2 |newspaper=[[Bangor Daily News|Bangor Daily Whig and Courier]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/bangor-daily-whig-and-courier-courtesy-v/120124556/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230927193229/https://www.newspapers.com/article/120124556/courtesy-vs-the-constitution/ |archive-date=September 27, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Sobel writes that Vose took over after Fairfield resigned, but this appears to be a mistake, mixing it up with Fairfield's resignation in 1843.|name=elect1842}}

|data-sort-value="363"|January 17, 1880{{efn|The 1879 election was not close, but at the time a governor had to receive a majority of votes cast, and Davis fell slightly short. Governor Garcelon refused to certify new Republican members of the legislature, instead seating Democrats, which led to the State Supreme Court ruling against him.{{sfn|Sobel|1978|p=618}}  A Fusionist legislature declared Joseph L. Smith the winner, and inaugurated him on January 17;<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 17, 1880 |location=Augusta, Maine |publication-place=Portland, Maine |title=Still Firm |page=2 |newspaper=[[Eastern Argus|Daily Eastern Argus]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/portland-press-herald-smith-inaugurated/131724198/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230918055332/https://www.newspapers.com/article/portland-press-herald-smith-inaugurated/131724198/ |archive-date=September 18, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> however, this was not considered legitimate, and Davis was inaugurated later that day when the Republican legislature met.<ref>{{Cite news |publication-date=January 19, 1880 |date=January 18, 1880 |location=Augusta, Maine |publication-place=Portland, Maine |title=Governor Davis |page=2 |newspaper=[[Portland Daily Press]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-portland-daily-press-davis-inaugurat/131724431/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230918050815/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-portland-daily-press-davis-inaugurat/131724431/ |archive-date=September 18, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>}}<br/>–<br/>January 13, 1881<br>{{small|(363 days; lost election)}}
